items.title: Pure water dissolves more silver chloride than salt water does
items.claim: Silver chloride is famously insoluble — Ksp is about 1.8 times 10 to the minus 10. But it dissolves slightly. Try to dissolve it in salt water and the solubility plummets to almost zero.
items.prompt: Why does adding more Cl- decrease AgCl solubility?

options.text: Le Chatelier — adding more Cl- shifts AgCl(s) is in equilibrium with Ag+ + Cl- back to the left, reducing dissolved Ag+ until [Ag+][Cl-] equals Ksp again
Silver chloride decomposes in salt water
Salt water becomes saturated with itself, leaving no room for AgCl

items.reveal:
Suppose in pure water solubility 's' equals square root of Ksp, around 1.3 times 10 to the minus 5 M for AgCl.

In 0.1 M NaCl, [Cl-] is dominated by the salt (about 0.1 M). [Ag+] must satisfy [Ag+] times 0.1 equals 1.8 times 10 to the minus 10, so [Ag+] is about 1.8 times 10 to the minus 9 M. Solubility drops by a factor of nearly 10,000.

This is exploited in gravimetric analysis: precipitate the analyte by adding excess of a common ion, ensuring almost everything comes out of solution.
items.why: Students think 'dissolved + dissolved = more dissolved'. Le Chatelier flips the intuition for ionic equilibria.

items.title: Mean bond enthalpies are wrong for the molecule in front of you
items.claim: Look up the C-H bond enthalpy: 412 kJ/mol. Use it to predict the energy to break the first C-H in methane. You will be wrong. Use it for the fourth C-H — you will be wrong again, but in the opposite direction.

options.text: The energy to break any single C-H bond, exactly
The MEAN energy to break a C-H bond over many molecules and many environments — individual bond energies for CH4, CH3, CH2, CH range from about 339 to 439 kJ/mol
The energy to make a C-H bond, not break it
The energy to break a C-H bond at 0 kelvin

items.reveal_title: Successive bond dissociation differs from the average
items.reveal:
Break one C-H in methane: 439 kJ/mol (to form CH3 radical + H).
Break the next C-H in CH3: 461 kJ/mol.
The next in CH2: 424 kJ/mol.
The last in CH: 339 kJ/mol.

Mean: about 416 kJ/mol — close to the tabulated value, but no individual bond requires exactly that. The values differ because each radical intermediate has different stability.

Bond enthalpy calculations of reaction energies are approximations that get within about 30 kJ/mol of reality — useful for trends, dangerous for precise predictions. Hess's law with measured enthalpies of formation is more accurate.
items.why: Single tabulated values look authoritative. They are weighted averages, and the value for any specific bond can be very different.

items.title: Bartlett made the first noble gas compound in 1962
items.claim: Until 1962 every chemistry textbook said noble gases were entirely unreactive. Neil Bartlett at UBC noticed that O2's ionisation energy (1175 kJ/mol) almost matches xenon's (1170). PtF6 had stripped an electron from O2. So PtF6 should be able to oxidise xenon. He tried it. XePtF6 formed instantly.
items.prompt: Why did this single result change inorganic chemistry?

options.text: It broke the assumed inviolability of the noble-gas 'rule of full octets' and opened the chemistry of an entire group of elements that had been written off as inert

items.reveal:
Bartlett's noticed PtF6 (a deep red solid) turned air red on contact: PtF6 had oxidised O2 to O2+ PtF6-. He looked up xenon's ionisation energy, saw the near-equality with O2, and reasoned that PtF6 should also oxidise xenon.

The synthesis (Vancouver, March 1962) used a gas-handling apparatus he had built himself. Within months, Claassen, Selig and Malm at Argonne produced XeF4 by simply heating xenon with fluorine at 400°C.

Today: XeF2, XeF4, XeF6, XeO3, XeO4, KrF2, ArF (the last only at cryogenic temperatures). Bartlett died in 2008. His insight made the chemistry of noble gases a real subject overnight.
items.why: Chemistry has 'laws' that turn out to be untested generalisations. A single decisive experiment can break a 70-year consensus.
